digest.intro: War targets AI stacks, math gets a proof engine, and cockroaches storm Delhi.

items.title: India's Cockroach Party Is a Real Political Force Now
items.blurb: The Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical, internet-native movement — has students, queer youth, and fist-waving women marching together demanding the Chief Election Commissioner resign over alleged voter-roll manipulation. It's not one protest; it's a dozen simultaneous mutinies (caste harassment at IIT Bombay, a gang-rape in Delhi, election integrity) that have found a single meme to march under. The name is the point: unkillable, everywhere, impossible to spray away.

items.title: Ukraine Is Bombing Russia's AI Training Infrastructure
items.blurb: Ukrainian FP-1 drones hit two of Yandex's five data centers this week, destroying the supercomputers used to train YandexGPT — a direct, explicit response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers that had knocked out mobile and internet services. Zelenskyy called it "symmetrical." This is the first time a combatant has publicly named an adversary's AI compute capacity as a legitimate military target and followed through.

items.title: The Middle East's Post-War Order Is Already Taking Shape
items.blurb: Middle Eastern oil shipments are back to 80% of pre-war levels despite Strait of Hormuz threats — a sign the U.S. is successfully degrading Iran's chokehold on the strait — while Iranian oil exports through the SoH have dropped to zero. Meanwhile Russia is escalating hybrid attacks on Eastern European dual-use logistics infrastructure, apparently to asymmetrically punish Ukraine's partners. The two wars are now influencing each other's pressure tactics.

items.title: Type 5 Diabetes: Recognized, Then Forgotten, Now Back
items.blurb: First described in Jamaica in 1955, withdrawn by the WHO in 1999 due to insufficient evidence, Type 5 diabetes — malnutrition-related, not insulin-resistant — has now been formally recognized by the International Diabetes Federation and they're pushing WHO to follow. The dangerous part: because it doesn't involve insulin resistance, treating it like Type 2 may actively harm patients, and it's thought to affect up to 25 million people mostly in low-income countries who've likely been misdiagnosed for decades.

items.title: Children Whose Gut Bacteria Stop Maturing Face Triple the T1D Risk
items.blurb: A Mass General Brigham / Broad Institute / Harvard study found that it's not the microbiome's composition that predicts Type 1 diabetes risk in genetically susceptible kids — it's whether gut bacteria keep developing over time. Children whose microbial communities stalled had three times the risk, a signal only visible because researchers sampled the same children repeatedly. A single snapshot would have missed it entirely, which is a quiet lesson about what longitudinal data can see that cross-sectional studies cannot.

items.title: Neanderthals Were Master Woodworkers — We Just Couldn't See It Until Stone Cast Their Tools
items.blurb: At Abric Romaní in Catalonia, mineral-rich water slowly encased Neanderthal wooden tools in limestone — and when the wood rotted away, it left perfect hollow molds. Spanish archaeologists cataloged 597 wooden remains spanning 62,000 to 40,000 years ago: spears, digging sticks, bark trays, shelter parts, and a club type never seen before. The whole reason we think the Stone Age was defined by stone is survivorship bias — wood was probably the dominant material, and this site is the only place geology accidentally preserved it.

items.title: Dead Prusa Printer Becomes a Liquid-Embedding Fabrication System
items.blurb: Riley took a Prusa i3 with a blown hot end, swapped in a syringe system, and turned it into an embedded 3D printer — extruding materials into a supportive liquid medium rather than air, which opens up soft robotics, bioprinting, and microfluidics on hardware most people would have trashed. The constraint (broken machine, no heat) became the exact condition needed for a completely different fabrication modality. Applications include printing biological tissue and flexible structures that would collapse immediately in standard FDM.

items.title: AI Coding Agents Make More Code, Not More Software
items.blurb: A Harvard study of 300 million work events across 700+ firms found that efficiency gains from AI coding tools are entirely absorbed by downstream review: pull requests require more revisions, reviewers leave more comments, and review cycles grow longer. There's "little evidence" firms increased software output or reduced headcount. The bottleneck isn't writing code — it's trusting it, and that's a human problem AI-generated volume makes worse, not better.

items.title: What Mathematicians Should Know About Lean — and What It Means That Fermat's Last Theorem Was Formalized This Year
items.blurb: Thomas Hales (guest posting on Tao's blog) argues that formal proof systems like Lean now represent mathematics' best guarantee of reliability — and three landmark formalizations completed this year (Navier-Stokes forced blowup, sphere packing in 8 and 24 dimensions, and Fermat's Last Theorem) have shifted the conversation from "can this be done" to "what does it change." The real question underneath: if a machine can verify any proof, what is mathematical intuition actually for — and who gets to decide what counts as understanding?

facts.fact: The WHO formally recognized Type 5 diabetes in the 1980s, then withdrew the classification in 1999 for lack of evidence — leaving an estimated 25 million people without a correct diagnosis for over two decades.

Ukrainian drones specifically targeted the two supercomputers Yandex uses to train its YandexGPT model, making this the first publicly acknowledged military strike aimed at destroying an adversary's AI training compute.

At Abric Romaní in Spain, mineral-rich water mummified 597 Neanderthal wooden artifacts in limestone molds — the only reason any of them survived 40,000–62,000 years is that geology accidentally cast them like bronze.

A Harvard study covering 300 million coding events found that AI coding assistants produce no measurable increase in software output, because the time saved writing code is entirely consumed by longer, more comment-heavy human code reviews.

India's satirical 'Cockroach Janta Party' movement already speaks of the sitting Chief Election Commissioner in the past tense — its protesters chant 'Gyanu, it's done, bro' — despite him still being in office.

art_picks.title: Playtime
art_picks.creator: Jacques Tati
art_picks.why: A city-scale system built to reveal how architecture shapes human behavior — Tati spent three years constructing a fake Paris just to watch people bounce off it. Every frame is a feedback loop between bodies and infrastructure; it will make you look at every built environment differently.

art_picks.title: Adnos I–III
art_picks.creator: Éliane Radigue
art_picks.why: Radigue spent decades composing on a single ARP synthesizer, building music so slow and structural it functions less like listening and more like watching a system breathe — obsessive narrow craft in exactly the way Willem responds to. The edge between physical resonance and electronic signal.

art_picks.title: Skyspace / Roden Crater
art_picks.creator: James Turrell
art_picks.why: Turrell spent fifty years reshaping a dormant Arizona volcano into a naked-eye observatory — the ultimate example of someone going unreasonably deep on one narrow thing (how brains construct light and space). His Skyspaces are the accessible entry point: a room that makes the sky feel like a screen.

events.name: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
events.venue: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1000 Fifth Ave, Manhattan
events.why: The first time these two are shown as actual equals at the Met — 120 works tracing two entangled practices, with the curatorial premise explicitly resisting the myth that one eclipsed the other; a rare chance to see Abstract Expressionism as a shared system rather than one man's heroic gesture.

events.name: Every Angel Is Terrifying — Dane Manary & Shayna Strype
events.why: A small, closing-soon multimedia show at one of Brooklyn's better off-radar spaces — the title alone signals the register (Rilke's terror-as-sublime), and Manary and Strype work in the kind of image-dense, layered territory that sits right at the edge of installation and world-building.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
events.why: Jafa's first US survey — two floors of film, sculpture, and image collage built around the proposition that Black popular music and Black visual culture share the same syncopated logic; the show is explicitly anti-austerity and structured like an archive run by affect rather than chronology.

events.name: Music for 18 Musicians: Staged Variations
events.venue: Park Avenue Armory, Wade Thompson Drill Hall, Manhattan
events.why: Three generations of musicians — Steve Reich's original ensemble, Alarm Will Sound, and students from Manhattan School of Music — perform Reich's 1976 masterpiece in a cycling durational staging inside the Armory's vast drill hall: a rare chance to hear minimal music as a living, spatial system.

events.name: Brooklyn Experimental Electronic Music Group — October Showcase
events.why: Free, late, Bushwick — four acts (Kelly Tsai, Parliament Cat, Beldame, CORS Light) doing experimental electronic and ambient work at a venue that sits at the exact intersection of arcade culture and underground music; low barrier, high weird.
